title: Chapter 1.1 — Solving Simple Equations
presenterNotes: Emphasize that keeping the equation balanced is the most critical idea. The analogy of a balance scale helps students visualize why they must do the same to both sides.
For real-life problems, walk through the four-step plan explicitly. Many students skip the 'understand' step and go straight to guessing operations.

examples.prompt: Solve $ x - 3 = -5 $ and check your answer.
examples.title: A – Solving with Addition
B – Solving with Subtraction
examples.peerPrompt: Explain to your partner: Why do we subtract 2.8 from both sides instead of adding?

explanation: An [[kw:equation]] is a statement that two expressions are equal.
A [[kw:linear equation in one variable]] has the form $ ax + b = 0 $, with $ a \ne 0 $.
The goal is to [[imp:isolate the variable]] using [[kw:inverse operations]].
[[imp:Addition]] and [[imp:subtraction]] undo each other.
[[imp:Whatever you do to one side, you MUST do to the other.]] This keeps the equation balanced.

rows.1: Add the same number to both sides.
rows.2: $ \text{If } a = b, \text{ then } a + c = b + c $

rows.1: Subtract the same number from both sides.
rows.2: $ \text{If } a = b, \text{ then } a - c = b - c $

visuals.title: Addition and Subtraction Properties of Equality

formulaCard.title: Solving by Addition/Subtraction
notes: Add $ a $ to both sides to isolate $ x $.
Always check your solution by substituting it back into the original equation.
formulaCard.formula: $$ x - a = b \quad\Rightarrow\quad x = b + a $$

confusionCorner.title: Watch the Signs!
confusionCorner.body: When a variable is subtracted, like $ x - 3 = -5 $, you must [[imp:add 3 to both sides]]. Don't subtract 3 – that would make it $ x - 6 $, which is wrong. Always use the inverse operation.

blocks.title: Equations and the Addition/Subtraction Properties

discoveryHook.scenario: Think of an equation as a perfectly balanced seesaw. If you add or remove weight on one side without doing the same on the other, everything tips over! Solving equations is all about keeping that balance while you uncover the unknown.

confusionCorner.title: Negative Signs in Fractions
confusionCorner.body: In $ -\frac{n}{5} = -3 $, the negative sign is in front of the fraction. That means the whole fraction is negative. Multiply both sides by -5, not just 5, to keep the sign correct.

blocks.title: Multiplication and Division Properties

rows.1: Multiply both sides by the same nonzero number.
rows.2: $ \text{If } a = b, \text{ then } a \cdot c = b \cdot c $

rows.1: Divide both sides by the same nonzero number.
rows.2: $ \text{If } a = b, \text{ then } a \div c = b \div c $

explanation: When a variable is [[imp:multiplied by a number]], divide both sides by that number.
When a variable is [[imp:divided by a number]], multiply both sides by that number.
The number you multiply or divide by [[imp:must not be zero]].
These actions are justified by the [[kw:Multiplication Property of Equality]] and [[kw:Division Property of Equality]].

formulaCard.title: Solving by Multiplication/Division
notes: Multiply both sides by $ c $ to clear the denominator.

confusionCorner.body: When solving $ -8r = 64 $, you divide by -8, not 8. A negative divided by a negative is positive, but here 64 is positive, so the result is negative. [[imp:Always carry the sign with the number you divide by.]]

formulaCard.title: The Golden Rule

explanation: To solve any simple equation, first [[imp:identify the operation]] being performed on the variable.
Choose the [[imp:inverse operation]] to undo it.
Apply that inverse operation to [[imp:both sides]] of the equation.
Simplify and check your answer.
Many everyday problems can be modeled with simple linear equations.
Use a [[imp:verbal model]] to turn words into math.
Define a variable for the unknown quantity.
Write the equation, solve it, and [[imp:check if the answer makes sense]] in the original context.

notes: $ d $ = distance, $ r $ = rate (speed), $ t $ = time.
Rearrange to solve for any variable.

rows.1: Identify what is known and what you need to find.
Write a verbal model or equation.

teacherCues: Pose the Usain Bolt problem: '200 meters in 19.32 seconds – how fast?' Guide them to write d = rt.
Emphasize the four-step plan: Understand, Plan, Solve, Check.

examples.title: A – Usain Bolt's Speed
steps: Understand: distance $ d = 200 $, time $ t = 19.32 $. Find rate $ r $.
Plan: Use $ d = r t $, so $ 200 = r \cdot 19.32 $.
Solve: Divide both sides by 19.32: $ r = \frac{200}{19.32} \approx 10.35 $ m/s.
Look back: At 10 m/s, 200 m takes ~20 s, close to 19.32 s.
examples.prompt: Usain Bolt ran 200 meters in 19.32 seconds. Find his average speed in meters per second.

explanation: The [[imp:Understand → Solve → Conclude]] blueprint breaks down any word problem into clear stages.
[[imp:Understand]]: Read carefully, define the variable, write the equation.
[[imp:Solve]]: Use inverse operations to isolate the variable.
[[imp:Conclude]]: State the answer in a complete sentence with units, and check reasonableness.
